title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 6: Midnight Chief Justice
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's March 28, 2010 Inquirer column criticizing De Castro v. JBC (March 17, 2010, 9-3), which held that the constitutional ban on 'midnight appointments' does not apply to the chief magistracy, clearing GMA to appoint Chief Justice Puno's successor

His historical case that the ban has always covered the judiciary -- judicially originated in Aytona v. Castillo (1962) on 'common sense and old-fashioned delicadeza,' written into the Charter on Commissioner Davide's suggestion to stop a President 'prolonging his rule indirectly,' and unanimously applied to the Court in In Re Valenzuela (1998, with Davide, Puno and CJP concurring)

The rebuttal of the pro-appointment argument: the 90-day deadline to fill a Court vacancy is 'legally suspended' during the ban (and even if not, ends Aug. 15, giving the next president 45 days), while the Judiciary Act of 1948 and a century of practice show an acting CJ routinely fills any gap

His proposed way out of the impasse: since the Court only directed the JBC to submit a list and did not command an appointment, GMA could heed her own candidate Gibo Teodoro and simply refrain from naming a midnight Chief Justice -- muffling public outcry and helping Teodoro's poll numbers
sub_topics: The setup: the JBC began vetting candidates for CJ Reynato Puno's May 17, 2010 retirement, against the constitutional ban barring a President from making appointments 'two months before the next presidential election, up to the end of his term' (save certain temporary executive ones)

De Castro v. JBC (March 17, 2010): voting 9-3, the Court ruled the midnight-appointment ban does not apply to the chief magistracy and directed the JBC to submit its short list 'on or before May 17, 2010' to enable GMA to appoint Puno's successor

Aytona v. Castillo (1962): the ban was judicially originated 50 years earlier, voiding President Garcia's last-day appointments (including one to the Court) on 'plain common sense and old-fashioned delicadeza,' despite no textual prohibition then

Davide's intent: the ban was written into the present Constitution on Commissioner Hilario Davide Jr.'s suggestion, expressly to keep a 'President (from) prolong(ing) his rule indirectly by appointing people to these sensitive positions'

In Re Valenzuela (1998): the Court unanimously ruled the ban applied to the judiciary, including the Supreme Court, instructing the JBC to defer filling vacancies -- penned by CJ Narvasa and concurred in by all, including three future chiefs (Davide, Puno and CJP), with Davide (the ban's sponsor) joining

The fifty-year consensus: this is how the ban was understood by Aytona, by the Constitutional Commission, by the people who ratified the Charter, by Valenzuela, and by all past presidents (including Marcos) -- now 'twisted' so GMA could name not just the 14 incumbent justices she had already appointed but also an 'Arroyo Chief Justice'

The 90-day rebuttal: the claim that the 90-day deadline to fill a Court vacancy overrides the ban fails -- Valenzuela held that period 'legally suspended' during the ban (and even unsuspended, it ends Aug. 15, leaving the next president 45 days); the Judiciary Act of 1948 and a century of practice provide for an acting CJ (the most senior justice) to fill any gap

The way out: the decision is seen as 'a craven effort to legitimize the wishes of the President' that eroded the Court's moral ascendancy ('the Arroyo Court'); since reversal on reconsideration is unlikely after a 9-3 vote, the 'easier way' is for GMA to heed Gibo Teodoro and refrain from appointing -- the Court having directed only that the JBC submit a list, not that she appoint

President Carlos P. Garcia (Aytona); Gilberto 'Gibo' Teodoro (GMA's candidate, urged restraint)
institutions: the Supreme Court and the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC)
laws_treaties: 1987 Constitution (the ban on midnight appointments; the 90-day rule for Court vacancies)
the Judiciary Act of 1948 (acting Chief Justice by precedence)
events: Puno's impending May 17, 2010 retirement and the 2010 presidential election

stances.claim: The De Castro v. JBC ruling is wrong: the midnight-appointment ban has covered the entire judiciary for fifty years -- from Aytona's 'common sense and delicadeza,' to Davide's express Con-Com intent to stop a President 'prolonging his rule indirectly,' to the unanimous In Re Valenzuela -- and that settled understanding is now being 'twisted' to seat an 'Arroyo Chief Justice.'
stances.rhetorical_move: settled-understanding argument: stacking precedent, framers' intent, ratification and uniform practice against a single 9-3 reinterpretation
stances.confidence: asserted with first-hand authority (he concurred in Valenzuela)

stances.claim: The 90-day deadline does not compel a midnight appointment: Valenzuela held it 'legally suspended' during the ban, and even unsuspended it ends Aug. 15 (leaving the next president 45 days), while the Judiciary Act of 1948 and a century of practice supply an acting Chief Justice for any gap.
stances.rhetorical_move: rebuttal-by-mechanism: dismantling the pro-appointment textual argument with the suspension rule and the acting-CJ practice

stances.claim: Because the Court only directed the JBC to submit a list and did not command an appointment, GMA can resolve the impasse -- and recover the Court's moral standing -- by heeding Gibo Teodoro and simply refraining from naming a midnight Chief Justice; 'it is really GMA's call.'
stances.rhetorical_move: off-ramp proposal: locating the practical solution in presidential restraint rather than judicial reversal
stances.confidence: offered as the realistic way out

notable_anecdotes: Garcia's last-day appointments: CJP recalls that Aytona v. Castillo (1962) voided President Garcia's appointments made 'one day before his term expired,' on 'plain common sense and old-fashioned delicadeza,' even without a textual ban.

Davide on both sides of the record: he notes that Davide both sponsored the ban in the Constitutional Commission ('to prevent a President prolonging his rule indirectly') and later concurred in Valenzuela applying it to the Court -- undercutting any claim the judiciary was meant to be exempt.

Even Marcos honored it: he points out that 'all the past presidents... (including Ferdinand Marcos)' obeyed the ban by not appointing to the judiciary during the prohibited period -- making GMA's reading an outlier.

The Teodoro off-ramp: he relays that GMA's own presidential candidate, Gibo Teodoro, advised her to refrain from naming a CJ -- a move that would 'muffle public outcry' and boost Teodoro in the surveys.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's March 28, 2010 Inquirer column, attacks De Castro v. JBC (March 17, 2010), in which the Court voted 9-3 that the constitutional ban on 'midnight appointments' does not apply to the chief magistracy, directing the JBC to submit its short list by May 17 so GMA could appoint Chief Justice Puno's successor. CJP marshals fifty years of settled understanding to the contrary: the ban was judicially originated in Aytona v. Castillo (1962), which voided President Garcia's last-day appointments on 'plain common sense and old-fashioned delicadeza'; it was written into the present Charter on Commissioner Davide's suggestion expressly to stop a President 'prolonging his rule indirectly by appointing people to these sensitive positions'; and it was unanimously applied to the judiciary, including the Supreme Court, in In Re Valenzuela (1998) -- penned by CJ Narvasa and concurred in by all, including three future chiefs (Davide, Puno and CJP), with Davide, the ban's own sponsor, joining. That understanding, honored even by Marcos, is now 'twisted,' he says, so GMA could seat not just the 14 incumbent justices she had already named but also an 'Arroyo Chief Justice.' He rebuts the pro-appointment argument: the 90-day deadline to fill a Court vacancy is 'legally suspended' during the ban (and even unsuspended ends Aug. 15, leaving the next president 45 days), while the Judiciary Act of 1948 and a century of practice provide for the most senior justice to serve as acting CJ. With reversal unlikely after a lopsided 9-3 vote, he proposes the 'easier way' out: since the Court directed only that the JBC submit a list and did not command an appointment, GMA could heed her own candidate Gibo Teodoro and refrain from naming a midnight Chief Justice -- muffling the public outcry against 'the Arroyo Court' and even boosting Teodoro's poll numbers. 'In the end, it is really GMA's call.'
